```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.retina = 2, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
has_stan <- requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(cmdstanr::cmdstan_path(), error = function(e) NULL))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_stan)
cols <- c(blue = "#4F6D8F", red = "#C8553D", gold = "#E0A458", grey = "#8C8C8C")
```

This vignette goes beyond fitting a single kernel:

* **varying slopes**: a regression slope that itself evolves along the
  tree, and how to tell it apart from a variance that simply grows with
  the predictor;
* **influential species**: exact leave-one-out for species whose
  importance-sampling estimate is unreliable;
* **prediction**: trait values for species without data, and ancestral
  states at internal nodes;
* **robust residuals**: Student-t residuals for data with outlying
  species.

All models here are fitted with Stan, so this vignette needs `cmdstanr`
and CmdStan.

## Allometry with an evolving slope

A classic question in comparative biology is whether a scaling
relationship, such as brain size on body size, is the same across a clade
or itself evolves [@lande1979; @pagel1989]. We simulate a tree of 120 species, body sizes evolving by
Brownian motion, and a brain–body slope whose deviation from 0.7 also
evolves by Brownian motion along the tree.

```{r simulate}
library(phylogp)
set.seed(1)
tr <- ape::rphylo(120, birth = 1, death = 0)
tr$edge.length <- tr$edge.length / max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(tr))
N <- ape::Ntip(tr)

set.seed(100)
body_all  <- ape::rTraitCont(tr, "BM", sigma = 1.5, ancestor = TRUE)   # tips and nodes
slope_dev <- ape::rTraitCont(tr, "BM", sigma = 0.5, ancestor = TRUE, root.value = 0)
body <- body_all[tr$tip.label]
resid <- kernel_simulate(k_bm() + k_white(), tr,
                         pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 0.6), white1 = list(sigma = 0.15)))
d <- data.frame(body = body,
                brain = 0.5 + (0.7 + slope_dev[tr$tip.label]) * (body - mean(body)) +
                  resid[tr$tip.label, 1])
true_slope <- 0.7 + slope_dev            # at every node, in node-number order
```

```{r plot-truth, fig.height = 4.6}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot_tree_values(tr, true_slope[tr$edge[, 2]], center = 0.7, lim = 1,
                 main = "True slope along the tree")
pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#24527A", "#7FA7C9", "#ECE7DF", "#E39A7A", "#A8322A"))(101)
idx <- round(50 * pmax(-1, pmin(1, (true_slope[seq_len(N)] - 0.7)))) + 51
plot(brain ~ body, data = d, pch = 21, cex = 1.2, bg = pal[idx], col = "grey30",
     lwd = 0.4, las = 1, bty = "l", xlab = "log body size", ylab = "log brain size",
     main = "Species, coloured by true slope", font.main = 1)
par(op)
```

## Three kernels, three hypotheses

We compare

1. a constant slope with phylogenetic and residual variation;
2. the same, plus residual variance that grows with body size, which is
   `k_slope("body") * k_white()`: species-specific slope deviations that
   are *not* phylogenetically structured;
3. a slope that evolves along the tree, `k_slope("body") * k_bm()`, the
   kernel form of a phylogenetic random slope in a mixed model
   [@hadfield2010].

Model 2 matters. A varying slope also makes the variance of brain size
grow with distance from the mean body size, so a varying-slope model could
win only because it captures this heteroscedasticity. Model 2 represents
exactly that alternative, without any evolution of the slope.

```{r fits}
f_const <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d, tr, k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
f_het   <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d, tr,
                    k_bm() + k_slope("body") * k_white() + k_white(), seed = 1)
f_vary  <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d, tr,
                    k_bm() + k_slope("body") * k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
f_vary
```

The slopes are fitted as latent values at the nodes of the tree, so each
gradient evaluation stays linear in the number of species. `body` is
centred at its mean, the reference point for the slope deviations.

```{r loo}
loo_vary <- loo(f_vary)
loo::loo_compare(list("constant slope"         = loo(f_const),
                      "heteroscedastic control" = loo(f_het),
                      "evolving slope"          = loo_vary))
```

The evolving slope predicts left-out species much better than both
alternatives, and the heteroscedastic control does no better than the
constant slope: the improvement comes from phylogenetic structure in the
slope, not from the variance pattern alone.

## Influential species

The flags above mean a few species have Pareto $\hat k > 0.7$: removing
them changes the posterior enough that the importance-sampling estimate of
their leave-one-out density is unreliable. `loo_refit()` refits the model
without each of them and replaces their contribution by the exact value
[@vehtari2017].

```{r refit}
loo_vary_exact <- loo_refit(f_vary, loo = loo_vary)
attr(loo_vary_exact, "refitted")
loo::loo_compare(list("constant slope" = loo(f_const),
                      "evolving slope" = loo_vary_exact))
```

The conclusion stands once the influential species are handled exactly.

## Where does the slope change?

`varying_slopes()` returns the posterior slope at every node, and
`plot_tree_values()` maps it onto the tree.

```{r slopes, fig.height = 4.6}
vs <- varying_slopes(f_vary)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_tree_values(tr, true_slope[tr$edge[, 2]], center = 0.7, lim = 1,
                 main = "True slope")
ft <- f_vary$tree
plot_tree_values(ft, vs$mean[ft$edge[, 2]], center = 0.7, lim = 1,
                 main = "Estimated slope (posterior mean)")
par(op)
```

```{r slopes-scatter, fig.height = 4.2}
tips <- vs[!is.na(vs$label), ]
truth <- true_slope[tips$label]
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(truth, tips$mean, type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l",
     ylim = range(tips$q5, tips$q95), xlab = "true slope",
     ylab = "estimated slope (90% interval)")
segments(truth, tips$q5, y1 = tips$q95, col = adjustcolor(cols["blue"], 0.35), lwd = 2)
points(truth, tips$mean, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = cols["blue"])
abline(0, 1, col = cols["red"], lwd = 1.5)
par(op)
c(correlation = cor(truth, tips$mean),
  coverage_90 = mean(tips$q5 < truth & truth < tips$q95))
```

Species-level slopes are shrunk towards those of their relatives, so
clades with few species and extreme slopes are pulled towards the middle,
but the pattern along the tree is recovered.

## Predicting species without data

Gaussian-process prediction on a tree is kriging [@garland2000; @rasmussen2006]: a species' value is
predicted from its relatives through the kernel. Here we hold out 12
species, fit the model to the rest, and predict them from their body sizes
and positions in the tree.

```{r predict, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(3)
held <- sample(rownames(d), 12)
f_pred <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d[setdiff(rownames(d), held), ], tr,
                   k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
pr <- predict(f_pred, newdata = d[held, ])
pr$observed_value <- d[pr$species, "brain"]
pr <- pr[order(pr$mean), ]

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(seq_along(pr$mean), pr$mean, ylim = range(pr$q5, pr$q95, pr$observed_value),
     type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l", xaxt = "n", xlab = "held-out species",
     ylab = "log brain size")
segments(seq_along(pr$mean), pr$q5, y1 = pr$q95, col = adjustcolor(cols["blue"], 0.5), lwd = 4)
points(seq_along(pr$mean), pr$mean, pch = 19, col = cols["blue"])
points(seq_along(pr$mean), pr$observed_value, pch = 4, lwd = 2, col = cols["red"])
legend("topleft", c("prediction (90% interval)", "true value"), pch = c(19, 4),
       col = cols[c("blue", "red")], lwd = c(NA, 2), bty = "n")
par(op)
```

For species that were fitted, `predict(fit)` without `newdata` gives
smoothed values that also use the species' own data.

## Ancestral states

Ancestral states are predictions at the internal nodes of the tree
[@schluter1997; @garland2000].
`ancestral()` computes them in linear time, averaged over the posterior.
Because we simulated the whole history, we can compare them with the
truth.

```{r ancestral, fig.height = 4.6}
f_anc <- phylo_gp(body ~ 1, data.frame(body = body), tr, k_bm(), seed = 1)
anc <- ancestral(f_anc, tips = TRUE)
anc$truth <- body_all[anc$node]
internal <- anc[anc$node > N, ]

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
ft <- f_anc$tree
plot_tree_values(ft, anc$mean[ft$edge[, 2]], center = 0,
                 main = "Reconstructed body size")
plot(internal$truth, internal$mean, type = "n", las = 1, bty = "l",
     ylim = range(internal$q5, internal$q95), xlab = "true ancestral value",
     ylab = "reconstruction (90% interval)", main = "Internal nodes", font.main = 1)
segments(internal$truth, internal$q5, y1 = internal$q95,
         col = adjustcolor(cols["blue"], 0.35), lwd = 2)
points(internal$truth, internal$mean, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = cols["blue"])
abline(0, 1, col = cols["red"], lwd = 1.5)
par(op)
mean(internal$q5 < internal$truth & internal$truth < internal$q95)
```

The intervals widen towards the root, where fewer descendants inform the
estimate. Under an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck kernel, `ancestral()` uses the OU
process itself; under Pagel's κ or δ, the reconstruction refers to the
transformed tree.

## Outlying species

Data sets of real species often contain a few values that no smooth
evolutionary model expects: domesticated species, measurement errors, or
genuinely exceptional lineages. Under Gaussian residuals such species pull
the estimates. `k_white(df = 4)` gives Student-t residuals instead: each
species gets its own variance multiplier, so an outlier is explained by a
large multiplier rather than by distorting everything else.

```{r outliers}
set.seed(4)
y2 <- 0.5 + 0.7 * body +
  kernel_simulate(k_bm() + k_white(), tr,
                  pars = list(bm1 = list(sigma = 0.5), white1 = list(sigma = 0.15)))[tr$tip.label, 1]
outliers <- sample(tr$tip.label, 6)
y2[outliers] <- y2[outliers] + 2
d2 <- data.frame(body = body, brain = y2, row.names = tr$tip.label)

f_gauss <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d2, tr, k_bm() + k_white(), seed = 1)
f_t     <- phylo_gp(brain ~ body, d2, tr, k_bm() + k_white(df = 4), seed = 1)
loo::loo_compare(list("Gaussian residuals"  = loo(f_gauss),
                      "Student-t residuals" = loo(f_t)))
rbind(Gaussian = summary(f_gauss)[2, ], "Student-t" = summary(f_t)[2, ])
```

The posterior variance multipliers point to the outlying species:

```{r multipliers, fig.height = 3.6}
lam <- colMeans(posterior::as_draws_matrix(f_t$fit$draws("white1_lam")))
is_out <- f_t$tree$tip.label %in% outliers
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(sort(lam), pch = 19, log = "y", las = 1, bty = "l",
     col = ifelse(is_out[order(lam)], cols["red"], cols["grey"]),
     xlab = "species, ordered", ylab = "variance multiplier (log scale)")
legend("topleft", c("planted outliers", "other species"), pch = 19,
       col = cols[c("red", "grey")], bty = "n")
par(op)
```

With Student-t residuals the slope estimate is closer to the true 0.7 and
more precise, and leave-one-out strongly prefers the robust model. For real
data, both models are worth reporting: the multipliers show which species
drive the difference.
